Mr. Speaker, the debate on CAP has been going on for a fairly long time now. Many people have used their time discussing the issue and how it would affect Canadians in general, how it would affect children and how it would affect the poor across this country.
My concern comes back to two or three issues that have to do with the CAP. First of all I think a program put in place that will cause very great hardship to many people in my area is an unfair program. In this case I look at what is happening with employment rolls and the difficulties in southwestern Ontario, not only the farm community problems but also difficulties with dismantling of manufacturing throughout Ontario. I quickly realize our welfare rolls have swelled and who has to pay the bill. Very clearly there are policies in place and bills have to be paid.
Government Orders
It seems very unfair that this government through a quick act, through a stroke of the pen, would say it is no longer responsible for the policies that have occurred in the past short time. What I am referring to is the fact that many of the policies carried out in the name of management by this government have created very difficult times in southwestern Ontario.
When we look at the free trade agreement, at the great promises that were made in it and at the results of that free trade agreement, we see that there were thousands of jobs lost, thousands of people out of work. We see children having a very difficult time of it. I see that for people in every walk of life. Whether it is small business, the farm community, the factory worker or big business in my area, the dollars are not there to support the economy as there were in the past.
The wardens of both Kent and Essex counties tell me that their welfare rolls have doubled, tripled and greater than that in some cases. In speaking about the numbers of dollars they require for social agencies to operate, their budgets have just skyrocketed far beyond their ability to pay.
In my community in Blenheim we have had a tax revolt which is the voice of the people saying that the taxes being imposed on them are far too strenuous in these times.
At the same time the federal government has created many of the problems with the policies it brought forward and is now saying that it is opting out of the bottom end of this whole thing by taking away support moneys to the programs put in place to help those in dire need.
I feel that the government really has put itself in a comer. As I stop and think about that I really wonder what type of managers the Tories are. I have to say they are poor managers.
When I was speaking a little earlier I heard three members across the benches suggest that the national debt when they took over was far higher than I recall the statements being. One member from Calgary suggested the national debt was as high as $206 million. Another suggested $220 million.
I have an inquiry that was sent to the then Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre. The question directly asked him what the national debt was in 1984. The answer he sent back was that the national debt

December 12, 1991
Government Orders
was $167,985 billion. The national debt in 1984 was $168 billion, approximately.
Our national debt today is skyrocketing over $400 billion which is well over 100 per cent increase. We hear week after week that it is because of the interest rates they had to pay back in 1984. Their spending was in excess of $30 billion beyond the revenues collected. They had to pay a national debt on interest of $22 billion which they attribute to past governments.
It is very clear in my mind that they not only spent $30 billion beyond the tax dollars they collected, but they did not point out at the same time that the government amounts received had increased to the point at which they have raised taxes since 1984 until today approximately one-third more than were available then.
If I were to take the government revenues in 1984 they were $64 billion. Today they are $128 billion. If I look at the government expenditures in 1984 they were $96 billion. Today they are $148 billion.
The government has spent a great deal of money on various programs and done many things it felt were directions it should carry out, but it did not consider where it was spending money or who it was supporting.
I have some real concerns that tax increases have been tremendous, that revenues have increased dramatically over the last six or seven years. At the same time the revenues increased it has built a $30 billion debt year after year on top of that. The end result is we are now sitting with an accumulated debt of well over $400 billion.
We do not have money to support programs that need to be supported and the government is saying it is fiscally responsible by cutting moneys that need to be spent on the poor in this country today, on welfare programs which are there to support most of our communities.
When I realize that it is just transferring that responsibility on to the provinces and on to the municipalities then I wonder what type of manager it really is. I believe that if it were responsible, the government would stop and look at the real basis for the programs it has.
I believe at this point that the government should start to examine how those overexpenditures are being created. We have to question whether building buildings or other projects under way are the things to do. Should
we be dealing with the poor, the weaker people in the economy, ensuring that education goes well, that lunch programs and schools go well, that those people who are having a very difficult time have the basic devices of life so that they can learn and increase their ability to be citizens in this community and are able to give as much as they can?
The direction we are moving in with this bill is retarding the ability of a great of number of people in this society to do the best that they can do. The problem is that we are not looking to the future. Presently we are looking at saving a few dollars, which create tremendous costs in the future.
Uneducated people, poorly nourished people who cannot learn, are going to be the children of the future if we do not change some of the things that are going on.
It is clearly evident that government has been very poorly managing our society. This bill is creating a tremendous disaster for the weak and the people who need support in our communities.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to this bill on report stage, Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan and the Motion No. 1 to delete clause 1.
Bill C-32 was given first reading on September 18, 1991. The bill will effectively extend the limit on the 5 per cent increases in federal contributions to British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario until 1994-95. These provinces are not receiving equalization payments.
This will prolong the agony even more by not understanding the call of the National Council on Welfare which says this must not happen. An advisory body of 21 members composed of present and past welfare recipients, social workers, lawyers, professors, people from all walks of life give a perspective and advice as a body to the minister of health. Yet, the minister of health of this government has turned deaf.
When the Supreme Court of Canada made its decision on August 16, 1991 saying that the federal government has a right to withhold its contribution it did not say that it should do it. The court only conferred the onus of that responsibility on the federal government. When that decision was announced the executive director of the Canadian Council on Social Development, Mr. Patrick Johnston, said: "The decision of the Supreme Court paves the way for the federal government to further limit
December 12, 1991

its financial support for essential social programs". This was said barely one month before this bill was introduced. The prediction and fear have happened already. First we allow the extending of the limit until the year 1994-95. It will only be a matter of time until it will be extended to the other provinces.
According to the estimate of this government, the three affected provinces were to lose $2,135 billion over the 5-year period anticipated in this proposed bill. Perhaps at this time of year this government may mellow. Perhaps in the spirit of Christmas it will see a miracle and change its heart.
I would like to review the background of the Canada Assistance Plan.
At the time of Confederation, assistance to those in need, such as the ill, the aged, the disabled and those who felt the consequences of family break-ups and were suffering, was given by charitable organizations and charities, at the time mainly in rural areas.
The Fathers of Confederation gave the social assistance jurisdiction to the provinces. However, it became clear in the 1920s and 1930s that the Fathers of Confederation were wrong. The obligation to help the poor and those in need is truly a national one. Hence, the Canada Assistance Plan was born in 1966.
A year before that, a great Liberal, Mr. Lester B. Pearson, gave his vision of how to help those in need in the throne speech. That is the Liberal vision which this Tory government is trying to erase from the map of Canada.
The Canada Assistance Plan has two basic objectives: to eliminate poverty and, at the same time and even more important, to prevent and remove the causes of poverty.
Who benefits from the Canada Assistance Plan? In 1988-89, 1.85 million Canadians benefited from the Canada Assistance Plan, of whom some 40 per cent, over 780,000, were children. Not only that, but the volunteers in volunteer organizations who help these poor children feel that there is recognition of their work if the Canada Assistance Plan is in place.
This government is trying to take that away. What message are we sending to our volunteers in the coun-
Govemment Orders
try? The Canada Assistance Plan has been described as a social bond, as the cohesive glue that binds our country together. What a better glue at this time when the forces of disunity are threatening to disrupt our country.
Through this amendment the government is violating the spirit of Canadian nationhood. It is violating the sacred trust of Canada's social programs. If this government pursues this amendment Canada would take a great leap indeed, but a great leap backward.
Also, the Canada Assistance Plan, in addition to the Guaranteed Income Supplement for low income pensioners, is the only remaining national program that explicitly fights poverty. It is a program for poor and modest income families to access child care services in the provinces.
As long as we still do not have the national child care program which this government promised in 1988, which until now has not been implemented, at least there is an escape in the Canada Assistance Plan and an escape valve for children in need of child care spaces.
This government is even trying to plug this escape valve. Where is the soul of this government? Therefore, at Christmastime I say: "Please, open your hearts. Rescind this amendment".
In conclusion, I would like to repeat that the intention of this government to amend the Canada Assistance Act is a great step backwards. Canada would make a great step forward if this amendment were rescinded. I support the amendment of the member for Essex-Windsor.
This morning the subcommittee on poverty tabled its report and the Liberal caucus decided to issue a minority report. Why is that? It is because the majority report of the government members completely ignored the sense of urgency to help our poor Canadian children. It completely ignored the witnesses that we heard over one and a half years who would like to have measures introduced for food, clothing and shelter.
We recommend a series of proposals, such as the establishment of a national nutrition-based program for breakfast, lunch and snacks and to immediately restore the entrance requirements and duration of entitlement

December 12, 1991
Government Orders
to the unemployment insurance benefits as they existed before Bill C-21.
We have asked the government to withdraw Bill C-20 and this Bill C-32. We would like an immediate job creation program this winter not next winter. You cannot postpone the temperature.
Finally we have asked that the federal minimum wage be immediately increased to $5 per hour. In the spirit of Christmas let us rescind Bill C-32 and we can go back to our provinces with a clean conscience and a conscience that we can share with Canada's poor.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House is disposed to have me speak for a very short time and I will undertake to do that.
It is seldom that I get the nod from my colleagues from the government side, but I suppose it is Christmas time and one is expecting to get some dispensation on these special occasions.
In all seriousness I did want to make a few comments on this bill. Essentially this cap affects three provinces. While they are outside the jurisdiction of my responsibilities as a federal member of Parliament I will say two things about that. While the cap does not apply to my province of Newfoundland, it does apply to three other provinces that are very close to Newfoundland in many ways. I am going to pick Ontario because as the economy of Ontario goes so does the work prospects of many Newfoundlanders who in the past would leave their homes, their residences or their towns to go and seek work in places like Toronto and other towns and cities in Ontario.
We felt the pinch of about a half a billion dollars if we total it all up in Newfoundland. This is because of a reduction in transfer payments in our case which reduced secondary and post-secondary education and hospital care. I have spoken on this frequently in the House and I am not going to repeat myself this evening. But this cap, as it applies to the province of Ontario and the other two provinces, concerns me greatly.
I do want to compliment my colleague from Winnipeg North who enunciated very clearly some of his concerns. The budget of February 26 was not the most popular
budget in the world. This is I suppose the last act of clearing up what is left.
If I could be permitted to finish in a civilized manner, I would veiy much appreciate it. I am not known as a heckler on this side of the House so I would ask the indulgence of my comrades across the way.
I think it would be worthwhile for us to remind ourselves who this is applying to and who it is going to affect the most. Who does this cap apply to? Well, I am going to just remind us, just before we close this session of Parliament, that they are the people that I come in contact with as a member of Parliament. I am sure all our colleagues come in contact with them.

Among those who benefit from public assistance and social welfare services are children in care or in need of protection because they are abused or neglected, the physically or mentally disabled, single-parent families, the elderly, the unemployed, families of persons in distress, low-income workers and battered women.

These are all types of people we have discussed in great detail in this House in the last session since we met here in early September.
I would have to be very strong in support of the amendment put forward by my hon. friend. I am not always known to support the other opposition other than the Official Opposition, but on this particular occasion I would find it very difficult in my heart to do otherwise.
On the basis of those who are affected by this I would be in support of the amendment. Before I do sit down I would like to also take the occasion to thank you indeed, Mr. Speaker, for your good guidance and judicious seating in the chair. I take this opportunity to wish that all my colleagues will put some of the things we have done in the past year behind us and hope that we can go forward with renewed vigour and with renewed purpose in the new year. Merry Christmas to all and to all a good night.

This ends our deliberations. I would be remiss if, on behalf of you all, I did not offer everyone who works for the House of Commons, from the Clerk to the humblest members of the support staff, in whatever capacity, my best wishes for a merry Christmas and happy holidays.

I would like to take a moment of the House's time to bring to the attention of hon. members the retirement of Mr. Aurele Periard, senior page, who has worked here in the Chamber since 1976.

I hope that his years in the House have not been too difficult and if his work load was heavy at times, we hope that it was made lighter by the energy and enthusiasm of hundreds of young Canadians.

I know that hon. members will wish to join me in thanking Mr. Periard for his many years of service and wish him good health in retirement.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I remind all hon. members that we will drink to each other's health right near here.
It being 5.30 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 28(2), the House stands adjourned until Monday, February 3, 1992 at 11 a.m., pursuant to the order made on Tuesday, December 10, 1991.
